definitions.definition: u_t(x,t)=∂u(x,t)/∂t, component by component. Derivatives are the usual real derivatives; a derivative not existing is assigned the total derivative convention value zero. When u is smooth on its open domain these are classical derivatives.
u_tt(x,t)=∂u_t(x,t)/∂t, component by component, with the same total derivative convention.

definitions.type: family indexed by j∈{1,…,n} of maps ℝ^n × (0,∞) → ℝ^m
definitions.definition: u_j(j,x,t)=∂_{x_j}u(x,t), the derivative along the jth standard coordinate direction, component by component with the total derivative convention. We also write u_j when the index j is explicitly fixed.

definitions.type: family indexed by j∈{1,…,n} of maps ℝ^n × (0,∞) → ℝ^m
definitions.definition: u_jj(j,x,t)=∂_{x_j}u_j(j,x,t), with the total derivative convention. The notation u_jj with fixed j has this same meaning.

definitions.type: family indexed by j∈{1,…,n} of maps ℝ^n × (0,∞) → ℝ^m
definitions.definition: v_j(j,x,t)=∂_{x_j}u_t(x,t), with the total derivative convention. With fixed j we abbreviate this by v_j.
Δu(x,t)=∑_{j=1}^n u_jj(j,x,t), the componentwise spatial Laplacian Δ_xu of the input.

e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|²+∑_{j=1}^n |u_j(j,x,t)|². Here |z|²=z·z is the Euclidean norm square on ℝ^m, so the spatial sum is exactly the Frobenius square |Du|². All integrals in the proof are Lebesgue integrals, and dx denotes standard volume on ℝ^n.

binders.type: vector in ℝ^m, locally bound in the norm-square identity

definitions.definition: e_t(x,t)=∂e(x,t)/∂t, using the total derivative convention, whose classical existence and formula will be proved.

inputs.statement: n≥1 and m≥1. The map u and all its partial derivatives are smooth on ℝ^n×(0,∞); in particular, for every x∈ℝ^n, t>0 and j∈{1,…,n}, ∂_t u_j(j,x,t)=v_j(j,x,t), and for every x∈ℝ^n and t>0, e_t(x,t)=2u_t(x,t)·u_tt(x,t)+2∑_{j=1}^n u_j(j,x,t)·v_j(j,x,t). For every t0>0, let J=[t0/2,3t0/2]. There exist a compact C⊆ℝ^n and R>0 such that C⊆(−R,R)^n, u(x,r)=q for x∉C and r∈J, and every positive-order derivative of u vanishes for x∉C and r∈int J. Put Q=[−R,R]^n, whose Lebesgue measure is (2R)^n. For every r∈int J the following scalar spatial functions are continuous, zero outside C, and Lebesgue integrable: e(·,r), e_t(·,r), u_t(·,r)·u_tt(·,r), and, for each j, u_j(j,·,r)·v_j(j,·,r), u_t(·,r)·u_jj(j,·,r), u_t(·,r)·u_j(j,·,r), and ∂_{x_j}(u_t(·,r)·u_j(j,·,r)). Their absolute integrals are finite, each bounded by a finite supremum on Q times (2R)^n. In particular e(·,t) is integrable for every t>0.

Let W be a complete real normed space and f:ℝ→W, with real endpoints a,b. If f is differentiable at every point of the unordered closed interval with endpoints a,b and deriv f is interval-integrable with respect to real Lebesgue measure from a to b, then the oriented interval integral ∫_a^b deriv f(z) dz equals f(b)−f(a).

hypotheses: W is a normed additive commutative group, real normed space and complete space.
f is differentiable at every point of the unordered closed interval between a and b.
deriv f is Lebesgue interval-integrable from a to b.

output.statement: For every t0>0 and j∈{1,…,n}, both integrands below are Lebesgue integrable and ∫_{ℝ^n}u_j(j,x,t0)·v_j(j,x,t0) dx=−∫_{ℝ^n}u_t(x,t0)·u_jj(j,x,t0) dx.

locals.declaration: Choose C from N002 for t0.
Choose its enclosing radius R>0 from N002.
Let ι(z,y) put z in coordinate j and the coordinates of y in the remaining positions in increasing order.
Fix arbitrary remaining coordinates y to evaluate the one-variable section.

argument.text: Fix t0>0 and j∈{1,…,n}; N002 gives n≥1 and the compact set C, radius R>0, and Q=[−R,R]^n. Define g(x)=u_t(x,t0)·u_j(j,x,t0) and d=∂_{x_j}g. They are smooth by N002. Apply M006 along the jth spatial coordinate line to the sections of u_t and u_j. The product rule gives d=v_j·u_j+u_t·u_jj. N002 states integrability of d and of its two summands, and also g=0 outside C. Since C⊆int Q, g vanishes on an open neighborhood of the boundary of Q, in particular at each pair of opposite j-coordinate faces.

produces.statement: d(x)=v_j(j,x,t0)·u_j(j,x,t0)+u_t(x,t0)·u_jj(j,x,t0). The three scalar functions in this equality are continuous, integrable, and zero outside C. The function g is smooth and zero off C⊆int Q, so it vanishes at the j-coordinate endpoints ±R for every choice of the remaining coordinates.

argument.text: Define the insertion map ι. Fix arbitrary remaining coordinates y∈ℝ^(n−1). The function z↦g(ι(z,y)) is smooth on ℝ and its derivative is z↦d(ι(z,y)). The derivative is continuous on [−R,R], hence interval-integrable there. Apply M003 with endpoints −R,R: ∫_{−R}^R d(ι(z,y)) dz=g(ι(R,y))−g(ι(−R,y))=0 by F001. These sections of d vanish when |z|>R. Thus their full real integrals equal the interval integrals and are zero. The oriented interval integral here equals the Lebesgue integral on [−R,R], since −R<R and the two endpoints have measure zero. This argument holds for every y; when n=1 there are no remaining coordinates and ℝ^0 is a one-point product with total measure one.

produces.statement: For every y0∈ℝ^(n−1), the section z↦d(ι(z,y0)) is integrable on ℝ and ∫_ℝ d(ι(z,y0)) dz=0.

argument.text: Under the coordinate extraction inverse to ι, M009 identifies Lebesgue measure on ℝ^n with Lebesgue measure on ℝ times the product measure on ℝ^(n−1). Use k=n−1, each coordinate space ℝ, and index j−1 in Fin n; n≥1 makes n=(n−1)+1. Hence the integrable function d from F001 has the same integral and integrability as (z,y)↦d(ι(z,y)) on the product. Apply M010 to that product function; its integral is ∫_{ℝ^(n−1)}(∫_ℝ d(ι(z,y)) dz)dy=0 by F002. Equivalently this is the supplied Fubini calculation over Q, since every term is zero outside Q and all terms are absolutely integrable. In particular ∫d=0. By F001 and linearity for integrable functions, 0=∫v_j·u_j+∫u_t·u_jj. Symmetry of the real dot product and rearrangement give ∫u_j·v_j=−∫u_t·u_jj, with all integrals finite. Arbitrary t0 and j yield the asserted integration-by-parts identity.
